lead: FGL (the FG loop peptide) is a 15-amino-acid synthetic peptide derived from the second fibronectin type III module of the neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM). It was reported to activate fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1), mimicking part of the signalling that NCAM performs when neurons adhere to each other [3][2]. It appears in longevity and nootropic peptide catalogues, where it is grouped with compounds that people take with the aim of supporting memory and brain ageing.

Its connection to appearance is indirect and runs through the wider longevity framing, in which sharp cognition and neural resilience are treated as part of ageing well. FGL itself has no published data on skin, hair, body composition or other visible traits.

Published research is preclinical: primary rat neuron cultures, neural stem cell cultures, and rodent studies of memory, social recognition, brain injury, ageing and Alzheimer's-type pathology [1][2][3][5][6][7][9][11][12]. No human clinical trial of FGL has been published.

angle.text: FGL is discussed as a neuroactive peptide for brain plasticity and ageing. Any benefit to how someone looks would be indirect, through the general idea of healthy ageing, and no study has tested appearance outcomes.

paras: NCAM is involved in neural development, cell migration, synaptogenesis and synaptic plasticity, and it signals through FGFR [2][8]. NCAM1 is a glycoprotein found on neurons, glia and skeletal muscle and is also known as CD56 [10]. FGL was reported to induce neurite outgrowth and neuronal survival in primary rat neurons [2].

In mice lacking all NCAM isoforms, basal phosphorylation of FGFR1 and of the kinases CaMKII and CaMKIV in the hippocampus was reduced, and FGL restored those levels, so that it mimicked NCAM's interaction at this receptor [4]. A 2016 review described NCAM and its polysialylated form as molecules associated with memory impairment, depression, autism spectrum conditions and schizophrenia, and discussed FGL and a related peptide, Enreptin, as NCAM-mimetic peptides able to restore disrupted plasticity in animal models [8].

A 2006 study reported that FGL promoted early postnatal sensorimotor development and enhanced social memory retention in rats [3]. In anaesthetised rats, FGL injected locally before high-frequency stimulation did not change basal synaptic transmission but facilitated both the induction and maintenance of long-term potentiation in the dentate gyrus [9]. Another study found it affected spatial learning impairment after neonatal phencyclidine treatment in rats, a model used for schizophrenia-like deficits [7].

In aged rats, FGL altered synapse and dendritic spine structure in the dentate gyrus on three-dimensional ultrastructural analysis [6], and systemic treatment modified age-related hippocampal changes, including loss of the presynaptic protein synaptophysin and glial-synaptic interaction [5]. In rats given a beta-amyloid fragment to model early Alzheimer's-type changes, FGL reduced neuropathological signs and cognitive impairment [1].

In adolescent rats subjected to cryo-induced traumatic brain injury, microarray analysis found that FGL treatment interacted with injury to alter genes regulating apoptosis, signal transduction and metabolism [11]. The 2016 review reported that FGL ameliorated depressive-like behaviour in NCAM-deficient mice and suggested it as a drug candidate for depression and other disorders of disrupted plasticity [8].

Chemists have also used the sequence as a building block. A 2008 study made a self-assembling FGL peptide-amphiphile that formed a nanofibre gel and examined its biocompatibility with neural stem cells in culture [12], and a 2022 ACS Nano paper attached an FGL peptide to a nanoparticle as a ligand for FGFR1, which is overexpressed at the blood-brain barrier, to deliver a hybrid mitochondrial peptide to cholinergic neurons in an Alzheimer's model [13].
No studies found in humans. The research described above is in cells and animals and does not establish effects in people.
FGL is not an approved medicine, and it appears in longevity and nootropic peptide catalogues. No community discussion of it as an appearance compound was found.

name: FGL

card.summary: A lab-made fragment of a neural adhesion protein with rodent memory data and no human trials or appearance evidence.
card.note: Preclinical only; no human studies found.

quick.overview:
FGL is a 15-amino-acid peptide taken from NCAM, a protein involved in nerve-cell adhesion and plasticity. It was reported to activate the FGF receptor.

Studies are in cultured neurons and rodents, covering memory, ageing and Alzheimer's-type models. No human trials or appearance data were found.
quick.mechanism: Reported to act as an FGFR1 agonist, promoting neurite outgrowth and neuronal survival in cultured rat neurons and changing synaptic structure in aged rats.
quick.risks: Human safety has not been established in published trials. It is not an approved drug, and animal findings do not establish human effects.
